headline.statement: Three reported means in this paper cannot have come from the data the paper says it collected: two Table 2 cells whose standard deviations no set of whole-number responses can produce, and a manipulation-check mean of 7.33 on a scale the Method defines as running from 1 to 7.
headline.evidence: Table 2, Self-evaluation row: "6.58 (.52)" and "4.08 (.52)" at n = 12 per cell (N = 96 over eight cells, corroborated by error df = 88). Experiment 3 Manipulation check: "the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001", against Experiment 1's "on a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely)", which Experiment 3 says it reused.
headline.plain: Ratings on these measures were whole numbers from 1 to 7, and that limits which averages and which spreads can actually occur. Two of the paper's reported spreads are not on that list -- no group of twelve people answering whole numbers could produce them. Separately, one reported average is 7.33 on a scale whose highest possible answer is 7, which cannot happen however the twelve people answered.

findings.title: Two Table 2 standard deviations cannot arise from whole-number responses, and they are the two halves of one reported contrast
findings.location: Table 2 (Experiment 3), Self-evaluation row, Positive mood / Unambiguous cue, Upward and Downward columns
findings.reported: "6.58 (.52)" and "4.08 (.52)". The measure is a single item: "Participants also rated their own attractiveness (How attractive are you?) on a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely)", which Experiment 3's Procedure says it reused.
findings.computed: grimmer_check, re-run at this stage on both cells: at n = 12 exactly one integer total is compatible with each mean (79 and 49 respectively), and for neither is there an integer sum-of-squares of the required parity that reproduces an SD rounding to 0.52 at two decimals. Both cells return failure_mode sd_granularity with feasible_ignoring_bounds = false and population_feasible_ignoring_bounds = false, meaning the failure survives under both the sample (n-1) and population (n) SD conventions and does not depend on the scale endpoints at all. Stage 1's SPRITE run returned no_solution_proven on the same two triples.
findings.assumptions: Two, both named. (1) n = 12 per cell is not printed; it follows from N = 96 over eight cells, is corroborated by the reported error df of 88 (= 96 - 8), and is further corroborated by all eight Self-evaluation cells being GRIM-consistent at exactly n = 12. (2) The value in parentheses is an SD, as Table 2's own caption convention and the rest of the paper indicate. R cross-check caveat, stated plainly: rsprite2 rejected both triples through its own GRIMMER screen with the message "The standard deviation is not consistent with this mean and number of observations", which agrees with our result in substance -- but it did so by raising an exception rather than returning a clean infeasible flag, and our wrapper measures a 16.2% false-raise rate for that path, so the R confirmation is substantive rather than formally clean. The finding therefore rests on our own analytic enumeration, which is a closed-form parity argument rather than a search that could have given up. Extraction was verified: the independently extracted PDF grid reproduces all 16 Table 2 cells identically, and the XML table was flagged neither alignment_uncertain nor image_only.

consequence.explanation: The 6.58-versus-4.08 contrast is the paper's evidence that positive-mood participants assimilate to comparison targets when the similarity cue is unambiguous -- the boundary condition Experiment 3 exists to establish -- and both halves of it are individually unreconstructable.

findings.plain: Each person in these two groups gave a single whole-number rating from 1 to 7, so only certain combinations of average and spread are arithmetically possible. For both of these groups the reported spread is not one of them: there is no way twelve people giving whole-number answers could produce that average alongside that spread. The two affected numbers are the two sides of the single comparison this experiment was designed to make, so the comparison cannot be checked and, as printed, cannot be right.

findings.title: Experiment 3 manipulation-check mean of 7.33 exceeds the seven-point ceiling the Method assigns to that measure
findings.location: Experiment 3, Manipulation check; scale defined in Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 Dependent measures
findings.reported: "the upward comparison target was rated more attractive (M = 7.33, SD = 1.19) than the downward target (M = 4.17, SD = 1.19), F(1,88) = 170.34, p < .001". Experiment 1: "Participants also rated their own attractiveness (How attractive are you?) on a seven-point scale (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely). Then, participants rated the target's attractiveness on the same 7-point scale." Experiment 2: "rated their own attractiveness and the target's attractiveness on seven-point scales (1 = not at all attractive and 7 = extremely attractive)". Experiment 3 Procedure: "rated their own attractiveness (on the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2)".
findings.computed: grim_check, re-run at this stage: failure_mode out_of_range, sum_in_range = false. The nearest admissible integer total is 352, giving 352/48 = 7.3333, but the maximum attainable total on a 1-7 scale at n = 48 is 336. The violation is independent of n -- no sample size rescues a mean above the scale maximum. The same paragraph reports a mood mean of 7.33, on a measure Experiment 2 defines as "(1 = negative mood and 7 = positive mood)".
findings.assumptions: The scale bound is stated -- Experiments 1 and 2 both print the numerals -- but reaching Experiment 3 requires one inference step through the sentence "on the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2", and that sentence contains a typographical error in the word "same". The innocent explanation is that Experiment 3 silently switched to a nine-point instrument, as its similarity items demonstrably are ("1 = not at all, 9 = extremely similar") and as the pilot's self-ratings were. What decides it against that reading: the Method sentence states the opposite, and all eight Experiment 3 self-evaluation cells in Table 2 -- measured on that same referenced instrument -- fall within 1 to 7, as does the downward attractiveness mean of 4.17. I record this at medium confidence for the inference step, and note that no GRIM-family R cross-check applies to a range violation, which is arithmetic on the stated ceiling rather than a granularity question. Either way the paper contradicts itself: either the mean exceeds its scale, or the Method misdescribes the instrument used for the paper's primary outcome.

consequence.explanation: This is the manipulation check establishing that upward targets were seen as more attractive, which is the precondition every Experiment 3 comparison depends on; the direction of the effect is unaffected, but the reported value cannot be what the stated instrument produced.

findings.plain: The paper says people rated attractiveness on a scale where 7 is the highest possible answer, and Experiment 3 says it used that same scale. It then reports an average of 7.33, which is higher than the highest answer anyone could have given. Either the number is wrong or the paper has misdescribed which scale it used -- and the sentence that would settle which is itself garbled, printing "seam" where it means "same".

findings.title: Experiment 4 control-group mean of 4.20 with SD .21 has no whole-number solution at any plausible group size
findings.location: Experiment 4, No load conditions and Cognitive load conditions, control-condition reference mean
findings.reported: "Higher levels of self-evaluations relative to the control condition (M = 4.20, SD = .21) were found". The control group's size is never printed.
findings.computed: grimmer_check, re-run at this stage at n = 15: the only compatible integer total is 63, and no integer sum-of-squares of matching parity yields an SD rounding to 0.21, with feasible_ignoring_bounds = false under both SD conventions. Stage 1 obtained the same result at n = 10 and n = 20 and SPRITE returned no_solution_proven at n = 15. The problem is that .21 is too small, not too large: the tightest whole-number configuration consistent with a mean of 4.20 -- a mixture of 4s and 5s -- forces an SD near 0.41.
findings.assumptions: The control group's n is never reported anywhere in the paper, and only n in {10, 15, 20} was tested, so this is not exhaustive; that is why it sits one rung below the tools' own `impossible`. The likeliest innocent explanation is a standard error mislabelled as a standard deviation -- a class of error found in roughly 40% of studies reporting an "SD" (Olsen 2002) -- and check_sd_or_se shows that reading implies an SD near 0.81 at n = 15, entirely ordinary for this scale and in line with every other dispersion in the paper. A simple typographical error is equally available. The paper contains nothing that decides between them.

consequence.explanation: This single control mean is the reference point against which all eight of Experiment 4's No load and Cognitive load contrasts are computed, so every one of those F tests is measured against a value that cannot be reconstructed from whole-number data.

findings.plain: The comparison group that every result in Experiment 4 is measured against is reported with an average of 4.20 and a spread of 0.21. For whole-number ratings, a spread that small cannot occur alongside that average -- the tightest possible arrangement of whole numbers would still be about twice as spread out. The most likely ordinary cause is that the authors printed a different measure of precision and labelled it a standard deviation, which is a common slip; but as printed the number does not work, and it is the anchor for eight reported comparisons.

findings.title: Error degrees of freedom irreconcilable with the stated sample size in three of the four experiments
findings.location: Experiment 1 Self-evaluations; Experiment 2 Manipulation check and Self-evaluations; Experiment 4 Participants and design versus Results
findings.reported: Experiment 1: "Female university (N = 47) students participated", with the factorial correctly at F(1, 43) but the simple effect at "F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011." Experiment 2: "University (N = 141, 75 women) students participated", with error df of 118, 124, 132 and 138 used across one experiment. Experiment 4: "University (N = 193, 103 female) students participated", with the three-way interaction at F(1, 110) and contrasts at F(1, 124).
findings.computed: Cross-reference reading of the printed df against the stated N and design. Experiment 1: a simple effect within the two unshared-birthday cells has roughly 22 error df, and even a two-group comparison using all 47 participants has only 45; the printed 46 exceeds every reading. Experiment 2: error df 118 over eight cells implies 126 participants, while t(138) implies 140, against a stated 141. Experiment 4: error df 110 over eight cells implies 118 participants in the factorial, leaving roughly 75 of the stated 193 unaccounted for by the single hanging control condition the paper describes. No exclusions or missing data are reported anywhere, and cell sizes are given for no experiment.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Part of the Experiment 2 spread is legitimately explained by the hanging control being included in the contrasts and excluded from the factorial, and I have not counted that portion against the paper. Ordinary listwise deletion would explain the rest but is nowhere stated. Experiment 3 is the counter-example that makes this readable rather than an artefact of my method: its df reconcile exactly (88 = 96 - 8 and 94 = 96 - 2), which is also what licenses n = 12 per cell for the Table 2 checks above.

consequence.explanation: Every test in Experiments 1, 2 and 4 -- including all three of the paper's headline interaction effects -- is reported on degrees of freedom that cannot be reconciled with the sample the same section states.

findings.plain: Every statistical test carries a number that records how many people contributed to it. In three of the four experiments those numbers do not match the number of participants the paper says took part -- in Experiment 4 about 75 people are unaccounted for, and in Experiment 1 one test claims more participants than the whole study had. The paper never reports how many people were in each condition and never mentions anyone being dropped, so a reader cannot tell how many people any given result rests on. Experiment 3 is the exception: its numbers add up exactly.

findings.title: Two reported F statistics fall below the range their own group means and standard deviations permit
findings.location: Pilot study mood ANOVA; Experiment 1 Self-evaluations, unshared-birthday simple effect
findings.reported: Pilot: "the mood manipulation significantly affected participant mood, F(2, 42) = 18.44, p < .001" with group means 7.20 (.93), 6.15 (.52) and 4.98 (.98). Experiment 1: "Exposure to the upward comparison target led to lowered self-evaluations (M = 3.33, SD = .65) compared to the downward comparison target (M = 4.64, SD = 1.50), F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011."
findings.computed: rivets_anova over the interval the printed precision permits. Pilot at 15/15/15: achievable F is [26.01, 27.04], against a reported 18.44; at 10/25/10 it is [22.20, 23.13]; at 8/29/8, an allocation implausible for three randomly assigned conditions, it is [19.99, 20.86]. The reported value sits below all three. Experiment 1 at 12 per cell: achievable F is [7.55, 7.89] against a reported 6.95, with zero of the Monte Carlo draws matching.
findings.assumptions: Per-condition sample sizes are reported nowhere in the paper, so the allocations are my inference -- which is why this is capped at `suspicious` rather than carried at the tool's own higher grade, and why I tested three allocations for the pilot rather than one. For Experiment 1, 47 participants do not divide evenly into four cells, so an 11/12 split would lower the achievable interval somewhat. The control that makes these interpretable: the same tool run on Experiment 1's manipulation check, with group sizes inferred the same way, returned `consistent` with the reported F of 38.80 sitting inside [38.39, 39.68]. Note the direction -- both reported F values are SMALLER than their own group statistics support, which is the opposite of what inflation would produce.

consequence.explanation: The pilot's claim that the mood induction worked and Experiment 1's symmetric-contrast result; because both reported F values understate rather than overstate the effect their own statistics imply, neither conclusion changes direction.

findings.plain: A test statistic can be recalculated from the group averages and spreads printed beside it. For two results, the recalculated value does not match what the paper printed -- and in both cases the printed value is weaker than the underlying numbers support, not stronger. Since the paper never says how many people were in each condition, part of the gap could be my assumption about group sizes; a third result checked the same way came out exactly right, which suggests the assumption is not the problem.

findings.title: Effect sizes of Hedges' g = 5.03 on a substantive outcome from twelve participants per cell
findings.location: Table 2, Similarity row, Positive/Ambiguous cells; Experiment 2 Manipulation check
findings.reported: "in the presence of ambiguous information, participants in a positive mood rated upward comparison targets as more similar to the self than downward comparison targets, F(1, 94) = 53.17, p < .001", from Table 2 cells 7.06 (.53) and 4.14 (.59). Also "Participants in the positive mood condition were more positive (M = 5.72, SD = .82) than the control condition (M = 4.40, SD = .83)", against a negative-mood mean of 2.98 (.83).
findings.computed: check_effect_plausibility: the Experiment 3 similarity contrast gives Hedges' g = 5.03, 95% CI [3.53, 6.88], pooled SD 0.561. The Experiment 2 mood manipulation gives g = 3.29, 95% CI [2.68, 3.96]. Separately, required_n: detecting even a large effect (d = 0.8) at 80% power needs 26 per group, against the 12 per cell this design provides -- a ratio of 0.46.
findings.assumptions: This is a reported magnitude, not a verdict, and an effect size can be improbable but never arithmetically impossible, so it is capped accordingly. The three ordinary causes were ruled out: dispersion is labelled SD throughout and its magnitudes (.53 to 1.19 on 7- and 9-point scales) are the size one expects of SDs rather than standard errors, which would imply near-zero variance; there is no waitlist comparator, these being randomly assigned laboratory conditions; and units match on both sides of each contrast. The n values are inferred, not printed. The Experiment 2 figure is a manipulation check, where very large effects are normal and unremarkable -- it is the Experiment 3 similarity effect, a substantive dependent variable, that is the outlier. No study in the paper reports an a-priori power analysis, so there is nothing to reproduce; the sensitivity calculation is asked of the paper's own cell sizes instead. That an underpowered design should return effects several times the conventional large threshold at very small p is the frame in which the rest of this review should be read.

consequence.explanation: Bears on how the paper's effects are weighed as a set rather than on whether any individual test is correctly computed; the similarity result itself remains significant on its own arithmetic.

findings.plain: The size of the difference between two groups can be expressed on a standard scale where 0.8 already counts as large. One of this paper's central results comes out at about 5 -- the two groups barely overlap at all -- from twelve people per group. That is not impossible, and I checked the usual innocent explanations (a mislabelled measure of spread, a do-nothing comparison group, mismatched units) and none applies. But a study this small has less than half the participants needed to reliably detect even a large effect, and effects this extreme from samples this small are exactly the pattern that publication pressure produces. This is my judgement as a reviewer, not a standard the paper agreed to.

findings.title: Experiment 1 asserts two significant main effects, prints a statistic for one, then denies the other one sentence later
findings.reported: "A 2(similarity cue: shared birthday vs. different birthday) x 2(direction: upward vs. downward) ANOVA revealed significant main effects of cue and direction of comparison such that those sharing a birthday reported higher self-evaluations (M = 4.92, SD = 1.14) than those not sharing a birthday (M = 3.96, SD = 1.3), F(1, 43) = 7.77, p = .008. No other main effects were significant."
findings.computed: Reading of two adjacent sentences. The design is 2x2, so it has exactly two main effects. The passage claims both are significant, prints an F for the cue effect only, and then states that no other main effects were significant -- which can only refer to direction, the effect just claimed as significant. No statistic for the direction main effect appears anywhere in Experiment 1, so the contradiction cannot be resolved from the text.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements.

consequence.explanation: The status of the direction-of-comparison main effect in Experiment 1 is asserted and then implicitly denied, with no statistic printed either way.

findings.plain: The paper says two effects were statistically significant, gives the supporting numbers for only one of them, and then in the very next sentence says no other effects were significant -- which contradicts what it just said about the second one. In a design of this shape there are only two such effects, so there is no third reading that makes both sentences true, and the missing numbers appear nowhere.

findings.title: Three of sixty-five reported test statistics disagree with their own p-values, one substantively
findings.location: Results sections, Pilot study through Experiment 4
findings.reported: "Identical effects emerged when the information was unambiguous, F(1, 94) = 1.50, p = .83." Also "did not differ F(1, 42) = .27, p = .76" and "neutral mood, r(24) = .53, p = .008".
findings.computed: statcheck over 65 extracted NHST results: 3 inconsistencies after a rounding allowance, and zero decision errors -- no reported p falls on the wrong side of the threshold it is judged against. F(1, 94) = 1.50 gives p = .224, not .83. r(24) = .53 gives p = .0054, not .008. The third, F(1, 42) = .27 with p = .76, reconciles exactly once the numerator df is corrected: recalc_f_to_p at df1 = 2 -- which is what a one-way ANOVA over three mood conditions requires, and what the companion mood ANOVA two paragraphs earlier correctly prints as F(2, 42) -- gives an achievable p interval of [.7609, .7685], containing the reported .76. That one is a typographical error in the df, not a wrong p.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The base rate matters and cuts in the paper's favour here: statcheck inconsistencies at roughly this rate are near-universal in honest work, half of the clean control papers in this project's own corpus contain at least one, and a rate of 3 in 65 with zero decision errors would not on its own support any adverse reading. Only the F(1, 94) = 1.50 case is substantive, and it is compounded by the sentence describing that result as "Identical" to a preceding F of .31, which it is not.

consequence.explanation: Zero decision errors: no reported p falls on the wrong side of its own significance threshold, so none of the three inconsistencies changes a conclusion the paper draws.

findings.plain: A test statistic and its p-value have to agree with each other, and a program can check all of them at once. Three of sixty-five disagree here. That rate is normal and would not by itself be a criticism -- most honest papers contain one. One of the three turns out to be a simple typing slip that corrects cleanly. The one that matters reports a p-value of .83 where the statistic gives .22, in a sentence that also calls the result identical to a different result it does not match. None of the three changes whether any finding counts as significant.

findings.title: Data offered on request rather than deposited, in a paper whose open questions only the raw data can settle
findings.reported: "Complete data and results available from the first author."
findings.computed: No computation applies. This is the paper's only data-availability statement.
findings.assumptions: Era context is decisive and is why this is graded `indeterminate` rather than as a defect: availability on request was entirely standard practice for a 2011 psychology paper, deposit was not expected, and this is recorded as an observation rather than a criticism. It is worth stating only because the specific questions this review leaves open -- cell sizes in all four experiments, the degrees-of-freedom discrepancies, the two unreconstructable Table 2 cells -- are precisely the ones access to the data would settle in minutes.

consequence.explanation: Changes no reported result; it determines only whether the discrepancies above could be resolved by a reader.

findings.plain: The paper says the full data can be had by writing to the first author rather than posting it anywhere. That was completely normal for a psychology paper in 2011 and is not a criticism of the authors. It is worth noting only because every unresolved question in this review is one the raw data would answer immediately.

The Stage-1 worklist flagged all 16 accusations with `quote_not_located`. That is a fact about the instrument, not about the findings: on re-reading the XML full text at this stage, every span checked -- the pilot ANOVA sentence, the Experiment 1 main-effects passage, 'F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011.', the Experiment 3 manipulation check, 'on the seam measures used in Experiments 1 and 2', the Experiment 2 participants sentence and the F(1, 94) = 1.50 sentence -- was located verbatim. The class is resolved globally and no individual finding was discarded on it.

This system reads one paper and reaches no network. Two questions a reader would want answered about a pattern like this -- whether comparable anomalies appear in other papers by the same authors, and how these effect sizes compare with the wider social-comparison literature -- are outside its reach entirely, and the interpretation is therefore partly ours and partly the reader's.

The article carries a retraction notice in its own title. That is recorded as context only. Nothing in this review uses the retraction as evidence; every finding above was derived from the paper's printed numbers and would stand or fall identically had the article never been retracted.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you supply the per-condition sample sizes for the pilot study and for Experiments 1, 2 and 4? None of the four experiments prints them, and several reported degrees of freedom cannot be reconciled with the stated totals -- Experiment 4 states N = 193 while its three-way interaction is reported as F(1, 110), which over eight cells implies 118 participants in the factorial.
questions_for_authors.why: Cell sizes are the single missing input blocking roughly 25 prose mean/SD pairs and all eight Table 1 cells from any granularity check, and they would settle the degrees-of-freedom finding directly.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you send the cell-level values behind the two Table 2 Self-evaluation entries reported as 6.58 (.52) and 4.08 (.52)? At twelve participants per cell on the single seven-point item, we can find no set of whole-number responses that produces either mean alongside a standard deviation of .52, under either the n-1 or the n convention.
questions_for_authors.why: These two cells are the two halves of the unambiguous-cue contrast Experiment 3 rests on, and both are individually unreconstructable from integer data.

questions_for_authors.question: Which response scale was used for the attractiveness ratings in Experiment 3? The Procedure refers to the measures used in Experiments 1 and 2, which are printed as seven-point (1 = not at all, 7 = extremely), but the manipulation check reports an upward-target mean of 7.33, and the mood mean in the preceding sentence is also 7.33 on a measure Experiment 2 defines as running from 1 to 7.
questions_for_authors.why: Resolves whether the reported means exceed their scale or the Method sentence misdescribes the instrument; the sentence that would decide it contains a typographical error ('seam' for 'same').

questions_for_authors.question: For the Experiment 4 control condition reported as M = 4.20, SD = .21, was .21 a standard deviation or a standard error? For whole-number ratings with a mean of 4.20 the smallest attainable standard deviation is near 0.41, whereas reading .21 as a standard error at a group size of around 15 implies an SD near 0.81, which matches the dispersions reported elsewhere in the paper.
questions_for_authors.why: This control mean is the reference point for all eight Experiment 4 contrasts, and the SE reading would resolve the discrepancy entirely.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you provide the statistic for the main effect of direction of comparison in Experiment 1? The Self-evaluations paragraph reports 'significant main effects of cue and direction of comparison', prints F(1, 43) = 7.77 for cue only, and then states 'No other main effects were significant.'
questions_for_authors.why: In a 2x2 design there are exactly two main effects, so the two sentences cannot both be true as printed, and no statistic for the direction effect appears anywhere in Experiment 1.

structured_output.report_markdown:
This paper reports a pilot study and four between-subjects laboratory experiments arguing that positive mood lets people reinterpret ambiguous information about a comparison target in self-serving ways -- assimilating to people who outshine them and contrasting away from people who do not. The design is consistent across studies: a mood induction, a comparison target, an ambiguous or unambiguous similarity cue, and a single seven-point self-rating of attractiveness as the outcome. The article carries a retraction notice in its own title; I note that as context and use none of it as evidence. Everything below comes from the printed numbers and would read identically had the paper never been retracted.

**What reconciled.** Twenty-six of the forty-three checks run came back consistent, twenty of them collapsed inside a single table sweep rather than reported individually, and several are worth naming because they are what make the failures interpretable rather than an artefact of method. Experiment 3's degrees of freedom reconcile exactly with its stated sample under both the factorial and the two-group planned comparisons (88 = 96 - 8, 94 = 96 - 2), which is the counter-example that gives the degrees-of-freedom finding in the other three experiments its force -- and which is also what licenses n = 12 per cell for the granularity checks. Experiment 1's manipulation check, with group sizes inferred exactly the same way as the two failing ones, returns a reported F of 38.80 sitting comfortably inside its achievable interval of [38.39, 39.68]. Table 2's sixteen cells were extracted independently from the XML and from the PDF and agree on every one. And across 128 cross-source comparisons, no duplicated mean/SD pair appears anywhere between Tables 1 and 2 -- these two tables are not copies of one another, and that is a clean negative result that deserves saying.

**Where the coverage stopped, and why it matters.** The paper reports cell sizes for none of its four experiments. That single omission is what blocks the largest part of this review: roughly twenty-five prose mean/SD pairs and all eight of Table 1's cells could not be checked at all, because GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE each need a denominator and substituting a guess is the fastest available route to a false accusation. Experiment 2 -- whose three-way interaction is one of the paper's headline results -- is consequently the least verifiable of the four studies. A further eight cells, the Similarity row of Table 2, were refused because that index is a mean of three items and our implementation cannot express the 1/(3n) granularity that requires; that is a gap in our toolkit and not a property of the paper.

**How the failures cluster.** What survives triage is not a scatter of small discrepancies. Three reported values cannot have come from the data described, and they are not in obscure corners: one is the boundary-condition contrast Experiment 3 exists to demonstrate, one is the manipulation check that licenses every Experiment 3 comparison, and one is the control mean against which all eight of Experiment 4's contrasts are measured. Around them sit degrees of freedom that cannot be reconciled with the stated samples in three experiments out of four, two F statistics falling below the range their own means and standard deviations permit, and a paragraph that asserts an effect and denies it one sentence later.

Two things pull the other way and should be weighed. The statcheck rate of three inconsistencies in sixty-five results, with zero decision errors, is unremarkable -- half the clean control papers in this project's own corpus contain at least one, and one of these three resolves cleanly as a typo in the degrees of freedom. And the authors correct their own multiplicity in footnotes 2 and 5, disclosing which contrast drops to p = .13 under Tukey HSD; that is straightforwardly good practice and it is not common.

Two of the three impossible values rest on a per-cell sample size of twelve that the paper never prints, though the inference is corroborated three independent ways. The third rests on a scale the Method prints in numerals but reaches Experiment 3 through a sentence containing a typographical error in the crucial word. Neither caveat dissolves the arithmetic; both are stated so a reader can weigh them.

The reported statistics do not reconcile with one another, and the failures reach the results the paper depends on.
